title: The resurrection and the life
hook: Jesus tells Martha: I am the resurrection and the life (John 11:25)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Koheleth, the Teacher who names a time to be born and a time to die. Your line was a time for everything.

A house in Bethany, near Jerusalem. A man named Lazarus has died. His sisters, Martha and Mary, had sent word to their friend Jesus while Lazarus was still sick. He came late. By the time he arrives, John's Gospel says, Lazarus has lain in the grave four days. Martha hears that Jesus is on the road and goes out to meet him; Mary stays in the house. Martha's first words are the ones a grieving person says at a hospital door: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died."
screen: `LAZARUS HAS DIED.` → `JESUS COMES LATE.` → `MARTHA GOES OUT TO MEET HIM.`

segments.voice: Martha already hopes. When Jesus tells her that her brother will rise again, she answers with what she knows: "I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day." Her hope is real, but far away, at the end of everything. It doesn't help much on day fifteen. Jesus answers: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." In John's telling, the hope Martha placed at the end of time is standing in front of her on a dusty road, with a name and a face. Then he asks her plainly: "Believest thou this?" Martha says yes, and names him the Christ. On the way to the tomb, before anything is mended, come two words: "Jesus wept." Only after the weeping does he call, "Lazarus, come forth," and the dead man walks out still wrapped in grave clothes. Christians read this as a sign, a return to this life. The hope they hold is larger: that because Jesus himself rose from the dead, the dead will be raised. Churches describe the details in their own ways, and in some churches this line is read at funerals and spoken at gravesides. Look back at the week: Nachiketa at Death's door, the fires on the ghats, a mourner's prayer of praise, neighbors who come to the house, numbered days, a time for everything. And today, one tradition's hope said out loud, whether or not it's yours.
screen: `MARTHA HOPES FOR THE LAST DAY.` · `"I AM THE RESURRECTION."` · `A QUESTION, THEN TEARS.` · `A WEEK OF ANSWERS TO DEATH.` · then, large: `CHRISTIANS HOPE THIS.`

segments.voice: Hear Martha's first line again, if you had been here, the sentence of anyone who arrived too late or watched someone else arrive too late. Then hear the answer in John's Gospel, I am the resurrection, and the life, and let it sit beside her grief, the hope and the tears in the same scene. If you pray, you can carry Martha's words into the quiet.
Martha, who met Jesus on the road after her brother Lazarus died and heard him say, I am the resurrection and the life. Today's word.
Your line: christians hope this. Hoping and grieving can share one road. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some churches read John 11 at funerals, and in some burial services the words "I am the resurrection, and the life" are spoken at the graveside.

chat.says: What did Jesus say to Martha after her brother Lazarus died?
options: I am the resurrection and the life. Then, on the way to the tomb, he wept.
Not to grieve, since her tears showed she didn't really believe in him.
That Lazarus would rise only at the last day, so she would have to wait.
chat.meaning: In John 11, Jesus answers Martha's far-off hope with I am the resurrection and the life, and weeps before he calls Lazarus out.

Bethany.meaning: a village near Jerusalem, home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus

Lazarus.meaning: Martha's brother, four days in the grave

Nachiketa.meaning: the boy in the Katha Upanishad who asks Death what comes after

ghats.meaning: stone steps down to the river at Varanasi

notes: No superlative used for John 11:35 (claims rule).
'This line is read at Christian funerals and spoken at gravesides' (and howItsDone 'in many churches'): confirm wording, e.g. BCP 1662 burial service opens with John 11:25–26.
'Churches describe the details in their own ways' is deliberately general (intermediate state, nature of the resurrection body).
Original left null: Greek anastasis was considered but no etymology is taught under the claims rule.

Audit: 'Jesus wept' moved from 'at the tomb' to 'on the way to the tomb' (John 11:34–38: he weeps, then comes to the grave) in the teach, match and myth; garbled practice line 'the answer John gives Jesus' fixed.
Editor: softened 'often read at Christian funerals' and howItsDone 'in many churches' to 'some churches' (claims rule); quotations checked against KJV John 11.
